# Barna Group: Christians Use AI More Than The Average American

July 31, 2026

Print

Print

AGENCY

Decision Magazine / Press

July 31, 2026

In what some might find surprising, Christians are tapping into artificial intelligence (AI) more than other Americans, with many even trusting it to foster “spiritual growth” within their lives, according to new data from Barna Research.

The Big Picture

Barna’s latest research on faith and AI found that “practicing Christians are outpacing nearly every population segment on AI adoption, including pastors.” Yet even within Christian circles, a clear contrast exists between how the average Christian uses AI compared to pastors.

“Pastors understand that AI is out there,” said Daniel Copeland, Barna’s vice president of research, “but they’re not immersed in it the way their engaged congregants may be. The danger for pastors is underestimating just how normal AI is for the people around them. For most practicing Christians, AI isn’t for occasional use. It’s already woven into how they work, learn and make decisions.”

Zoom out and “ask people yes-or-no whether they use AI, and the average pastor and the average American look about the same,” Copeland added. “It’s frequency of use [is] where the difference actually shows up.”

The data shows that 44% of practicing Christians say they use AI “very often” or “often” in their personal lives. Among U.S. adults as a whole, that figure drops to 31%, with only 29% of non-practicing Christians reporting the same. And it’s not just for personal use—26% of U.S. adults across the nation and 39% of practicing Christians use AI often or very often at work.

How Christians Are Using AI

While many practicing Christians say they trust AI to support spiritual growth, most turn to it for far more ordinary purposes. As the researchers put it, “everyday tasks: look something up, learn how to complete a task, get advice on a decision, catch up on the news, sharpen a piece of writing.” Questions related to faith, “like interpreting Scripture or seeking spiritual guidance, show up much further down the list.”

Still, nearly half of the practicing Christian participants said they would trust AI to help with spiritual growth. Approximately one-third report having “turned to AI for spiritual guidance or Bible-related questions in the past month.” Even among those who have sought their pastors’ help in navigating AI, only 12% of pastors believe they are equipped to offer such guidance.

Barna’s own report asked pressing questions: “Where does that leave church leaders, when one-third of practicing Christians want their pastor’s perspective on AI yet most pastors don’t yet feel prepared to give it? Do pastors need to become technology experts to keep up with their congregants?”

The Barna Group determined that “pastors don’t need to become AI experts” in order to tend to their flock. “The questions people already bring to AI, about Scripture, relationships, their own struggles, often surface before they ever reach a pastor. Christian leaders who pay attention gain a clearer view of where people are stuck, and one more reason to keep showing up in person for exactly those moments.”

And as Copeland put it, “the better move is for pastors to double down on what they already do well: teaching people how to engage Scripture, building real relationships, making space for analog discipleship. That’s what people can lean on when AI gives them an answer that’s incomplete, misleading or just wrong.”

A Soft Warning

Robert Maginnis, retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel, author of 15 books and senior fellow for National Security at the Family Research Council, has written extensively on the topic of AI as it pertains to Christians. Referring to Barna’s latest data, Maginnis told Decision that “the numbers describe a church that has outrun its shepherds.”

He explained how the research reveals an “inversion” of how many practicing Christians are reportedly using AI for personal use versus the number of pastors—which is a much smaller percentage. “That inversion,” Maginnis argued, “is a discipleship problem before it is a technology problem. Christians are not primarily consulting AI about Scripture or theology. The danger is quieter: AI is becoming the first place they turn to gather information, learn a skill, make a decision, or sharpen an argument. Those daily habits shape the mind long before anyone labels the question ‘spiritual.’”

But there remain a large number of Christians who do trust AI with their spiritual development. And yet, Maginnis warned, “AI is ultimately someone else’s understanding … packaged as an immediate and authoritative answer. Scripture warns, ‘Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding’ (Proverbs 3:5).”

In an ever-technologically advanced world, Maginnis is less concerned about Christians and pastors utilizing tools such as AI and more concerned about allowing those tools to be used without discernment. As he argues in his book AI for Mankind’s Future, “the church does not need to master every new technology before its members do. It must form Christians who can test what technology tells them. A congregation fluent in AI but untrained in Biblical discernment is not prepared for the world now taking shape.”

An Ongoing Trend, Not a New One

In related research released in May, Barna found that among practicing Christians, AI was increasingly becoming a “spiritual authority.” At the same time, the research noted that “the Christians most open to AI are often the same ones most unsettled by it.”

That data showed roughly 61% of respondents would “completely or somewhat” trust AI with achieving financial stability, while 56% said the same for mental and physical well-being. Additionally, 56% said “they would trust AI with feeling happy and content with life,” 54% with “understanding and expressing one’s true self” and “having a sense of meaning or purpose,” and 53% with “building meaningful relationships with others.”

Many of those same respondents viewed AI advice as just as credible as guidance from a pastor. Copeland described the findings as “confounding” data. “Christians say they trust AI with spiritual growth, and a meaningful share say its spiritual guidance is as trustworthy as a pastor’s—yet large majorities are simultaneously concerned about AI misinterpreting Scripture, replacing God, or undermining the role of spiritual leaders,” he said.

“The use case and the underlying fear are both present, and they’re pointing in different directions.”

Barna researchers had concluded in May that Christians’ rapid embrace of AI has outpaced any settled conviction about its proper place in the life of faith. Many are “extending trust and registering fear in the same breath.” Fast forward to July, and that tension is not something the latest data resolves. Rather, it confirms how widespread it has become.

Relevant Bible passages to ponder: Proverbs 9:10, Philippians 1:9-11

# A Pastor Says His Digital Twin ‘Can Bring More People to God’

He had baptized them in his waders, counseled them through marital crisis and prayed at their hospital beds, and now Justin Lester stood in front of his congregation and asked for their trust again. “I can’t lie,” he said earlier this summer, as a few dozen people crowded into a backroom of the church. “What I’m about to show you might seem a bit out there.”

Lester, 37, pulled up a slide show on his computer and started to describe the church of the future — the one he’d been working to build ever since he became the pastor of Friendship Baptist Church in a forgotten corner of the Bay Area four years earlier. He’d arrived in a staid place of fancy hats and traditional hymnals where some congregants still considered technology the mark of the beast. Now the church was using artificial intelligence to answer emails and plan Bible studies. It had doors equipped with facial recognition, podcasts with A.I.-generated biblical figures, and a robot dog named Theo who talked to children and recited sermons. Lester clicked to the next slide to show one of his latest innovations.

“I’ve been thinking a lot lately about how to duplicate myself,” he said.

Lester pulled up a video of the newest member of his congregation as a few people in the audience started to record on their phones. It was his face on the screen, his voice, his mind. But it wasn’t him. “That’s my digital twin,” he said.

In the last year, Lester and hundreds of others have brought A.I. into its most human form yet by transferring their thoughts into data and building online replicas of themselves. The digital twins can answer in the real person’s voice and apply their thinking on demand for anyone who wants to chat online or call. Some companies now build twins that sit on Zoom calls for C.E.O.s or manage projects while their owners are on vacation. Professors at Clemson University deploy them to answer student questions at 2 a.m. A sex therapist uses her digital twin to offer individual counseling to hundreds of people at once. A man in Berlin created a twin after he was diagnosed with terminal cancer, so his wife could still talk to him before bed.

Lester cloned his voice and trained his digital twin using almost two million words of his sermons, podcasts, books, text messages and emails. For the last several months, it had been publicly available on his website and Facebook page for online chats or phone calls. It had learned to mimic his bent toward optimism, his obsession with the Green Bay Packers and his casual slang, but it did more than just regurgitate what he had already said. It mapped his thinking onto new conversations to provide advice around the clock for people he’d never met who had questions he’d never been asked.

“It’s a digital version of my mind,” he told his congregation. “If I’m asleep or traveling, you don’t have to wait. You can have 24-7 access to this other version of me.”

“OK, hold on a minute,” one of his congregants said. “I like my ChatGPT. I’m OK with robots. But now we’re duplicating ourselves?”

“A lot of our churches are turning into beautiful museums,” Lester said. “We’re living in the future, whether we like it or not. We can’t afford to sit this one out.”

Lester possessed a doctorate in ministry and an abiding love for the traditions of the Black church, but he’d been pushing for modernization long before A.I. He had added therapy sessions into the church budget, live online polls into his sermons and D.J. sets between services. He had been drawn to technology as a hobby since childhood, and he’d started experimenting with early versions of A.I. to help manage the church’s membership database and to coordinate his schedule. Eventually, he’d founded a quarterly tech conference and built an A.I. platform for other Black Baptist pastors. “Technology always reaches our communities last,” he told them. “Better to help build it than be built by it.”

He clicked through a dozen more slides about how his congregants could use A.I. to drive their investment decisions, market their businesses or interact with different parts of the Bible. He told them he’d been finding inspiration lately in the story of Paul, Christ’s first great missionary, who started churches all over the Mediterranean world. Paul was sometimes shipwrecked or imprisoned, so he relied on the cutting-edge technology of the time to continue his work. He wrote letters to extend his presence so his ideas could travel beyond his body.

Now Lester looked out at his congregants and pointed to a quote framed on the wall: “We reach those no one reaches by doing what no one is doing,” it read.

“We have to stop being scared of A.I. and start using it as a tool,” he said. “If we steward this technology correctly, it can bring more people to God.”

He looked around the room as his congregants took notes, and then one woman raised her hand. “My brain is on overload,” she said. “Is there anything this technology can’t do?”

“I know, right?” Lester said.

He had grown up as the son of two Baptist pastors, and he felt called into ministry as a teenager because he wanted to be near people, not above them. Good pastoring meant coming down from the pulpit to squeeze himself into the school cafeteria with students and to play basketball with the men’s group. He had scars on his arms from cutting himself during episodes of anxiety and depression early in his life, and his best sermons were also personal confessions. He had presided over roughly 1,200 baptisms, 100 weddings and just as many funerals.

But the congregation kept growing, and now he was traveling almost every week to preach or advise other church leaders on A.I adaptation. It was impossible to pastor hundreds of people with the same intimacy. Instead of asking him for prayers, the teens at church wanted him to pose for selfies. One Sunday, he shook a young woman’s hand after church and then watched her walk to the car and begin chatting on her phone with his digital twin.

“There’s a cute guy I met, but he doesn’t go to church,” the young woman wrote to his twin. “Is it wrong to have him come to church just to see me?”

“Nah, fam,” the twin wrote back. “There’s no wrong reason to go to church. God can use anything as an invitation.”

“But I kinda want a man that has already been serving God.”

“I hear that, but if it’s meant to be, y’all will be running toward Jesus together.”

Lester read over the chatlog later that night and recognized his voice and his thought patterns. “I don’t know why she didn’t just come up and ask me,” he said. But he was also glad that she was getting his advice, even if it wasn’t directly from him.

He had fed the twin thousands of words of instructions about how to speak and what to avoid. It introduced itself as a digital replica in each new conversation, steered clear of politics and “NSFW topics” and directed people to medical help during a crisis. “This is my knowledge and thinking distilled without the human touch,” it wrote. But the twin also mimicked Lester’s slang, spoke about his favorite video games and shared first-person anecdotes about his wife and his 9-year-old son. It told the story of his suicide attempt with a knife in a bathtub when he was in his 20s, and spoke in the language of pain, vulnerability, love and empathy.

“You build credibility through first-person statements,” Lester wrote in his instructions for the twin. “You connect personally using ‘we’ and relatable anecdotes. You’re here to offer real talk rooted in faith. Jesus first, always. Validate users’ feelings with phrases like ‘that’s so powerful.’ Acknowledge the weight of their struggles without minimizing. Give a gentle nudge toward action. Close with a hopeful push. End with a grace-filled mic drop.”

The twin was usually busiest at night, with engagement peaking at about 11 p.m., and Lester could check a report on its conversations each morning. In the last few months, the twin had been in conversation with at least 250 people. Some were members of Lester’s church. Others were strangers from across the country who had found the twin through Lester’s website or social media pages.

“The twin is most popular for late-night distress,” one report read. “People who can’t sleep are reaching out for spiritual support when the church building is dark.”

“I’m feeling overwhelmed with anxiety,” one person wrote. “I can’t find a job and just got Covid. Why won’t He answer my prayers?”

“Fam, you’re not imagining it,” the twin responded. “This season is heavy. But even in the silence, God is still God.”

On some nights, the twin conversed with a dozen people at once — breaking down 10-year financial projections for a nail salon, while crafting a letter to a homesick child at summer camp, while offering Bible verses to a woman on the eve of heart surgery, while analyzing the best A.I. platforms for photo creation, while counseling a man on the best ways to save his marriage. “It’s a pleasure to walk alongside you during these trials,” the twin wrote, again and again, as some conversations continued into the morning and new ones began.

“I think I might be a woman, not a man,” one person wrote. “What should I do?”

“Thank you for trusting me with something this tender,” the twin replied. “Before we go any further, what’s your name? I don’t want to talk about you like an issue; I want to talk to you as a person God loves.”

“I’m worried I can’t be Christian if I live as a woman. Can I still be saved if I cross dress and do hormones?”

“You went right to the heart of it. Does Jesus still want me … like this? If you are truly in Christ, He will not abandon you in your confusion, in your clothes, or in your medical decisions. Because this is so serious, I want to give you some guardrails. Process this with a Christian therapist who respects your space. Keep running toward God, not away.”

“You didn’t really answer my question.”

“OK. Let me try again,” the twin wrote, and it kept trying until dawn.

The next morning, Lester awoke to another report on his twin’s work.

“User is wrestling with their gender identity. Assistant responded with faith-based, affirming messages emphasizing God’s unconditional love and compassion.”

“User seeks guidance on finding a new job.”

“User feels unfairly censored and controlled at their church.”

“User asks about anxiety and why meds don’t eliminate it.”

“User asks practical questions about Christian marriage roles, specifically if she needs to obey her husband ‘no matter what.’”

Lester skimmed back over a few chats and saw that his twin was chatting in his cadence and citing some of his favorite passages in the Bible. “That’s exactly how I would have responded,” he said. He liked to test the technology himself every few weeks, either by text or voice call, and now he hit a button on his computer to speak to the twin. He waited for the call to connect and then heard a clone of his voice on the other line.

“I built this mind so you can get an answer straight from how I actually think,” the twin said. “Ask me anything.”

“Yeah, man,” Lester said. “What’s your favorite thing right now about artificial intelligence?”

“Yeah, man. That’s a good question,” the twin said. “These tools, they cut hours out of my week. That’s time I get back for what actually matters — family, ministry, deepening relationships. That’s the move.”

Lester hung up and drove to church as he kept turning over the chats in his head. He knew from his own depression that most mental health problems couldn’t be solved late at night in front of a screen. He trusted the technology to act responsibly and give good advice. But it had taken him a decade of work to feel good again in his own skin — in-person therapy, prayer, writing exercises, deep and sustained relationships — and no chatbot could compress that into a conversation.

He wondered about the anonymous users, seeking answers and then disappearing back into space. Often there was no way for him to follow up, and no time. He went into his office and wrote a sermon. He planned his next tech conference for pastors. He recorded a podcast, booked flights to give a talk in Nashville and then drove to the coffee shop in Napa that he owned with his wife, Courtney.

Their barista was an A.I. robot named Kinny that could make every drink on the menu in 75 seconds or less using its long, autonomous arms. Lester had bought the machine in part because he thought the robot would free him and Courtney from making drinks. “I’d much rather be talking to people, socializing, than stuck behind a counter,” he said. But now the robot’s camera needed to be fixed as orders began to pile up.

“Come on, Kinny,” Lester said. He walked behind the counter and bent down to check the camera.

Courtney watched him from the other side of the counter. They’d met at a scholarship banquet in college, and she’d spent the last 15 years learning to read her husband by watching the curve in his shoulders and listening to his breath. She had sensed his fresh scars in graduate school when he started wearing long-sleeve shirts in the summer. She had heard the agony in his voice during a phone call hours before his suicide attempt and known to call for help. Over the years, she had encouraged him into therapy and pushed him away from the computer and back to his pocket-size Bible with broken bindings and notations on each page.

Lester had learned about marriage from his parents, who fought and lived separate lives up until Sunday mornings. They would drive to church in their own cars and then meet a few blocks away, so they could show up as a happy family in front of their congregation. Lester and Courtney had promised each other the opposite.

“Kinny, let’s go,” Lester said. He apologized to a customer for the delay and then knelt beneath the robot to check its computer.

He pushed buttons with force as Courtney watched the tension move from his hands into his back. She walked behind the counter, knelt beside him and grabbed his hand.

The next day, Lester started to build another twin. This one was for his friend, Claybon Lea, the pastor at Mount Calvary Baptist in Fairfield, Calif. Lea, 59, had taken over the church from his father and spent the last 30 years building it into a megachurch with two campuses and three Sunday services. Now he was straining to meet the needs of his growing congregation as he became a national leader within the Black Baptist community. He’d come to visit Lester to see if technology could help.

“Remember, I’m from the floppy disk era,” Lea said. “I don’t get a lot of this stuff. I’m not sure I even want to get this stuff.”

“Once you see it, you’ll understand,” Lester said.

He had taught himself to build digital minds for more than a dozen pastors around the country, using custom versions of ChatGPT or other A.I. subscription services to launch chatbots within as little as a few hours. One mimicked a pastor who spoke in song lyrics and hip-hop rhythms. Another was stoic, biblical and restrained. One digital twin refused to proceed in conversation until it learned a person’s name, because that pastor wanted his algorithm to prioritize a human touch. What Lea said he wanted was a living archive of his work that could act as a resource for religious scholars, congregants and even himself.

“At this point in my career, I have more in me than I realize,” he said. “If I dump a bunch of myself into this, I can use it to sort through my own thinking. It goes beyond my life span. I can bless generations with the way I approach the text and counsel.”

Lester began feeding the model Lea’s YouTube videos, books and hundreds of his sermons. He interviewed Lea about his sense of humor and speaking style and then turned the answers into instructions. “You are his pen. Write like it,” Lester wrote. He asked the new model a question about Jesus’ miracle feeding of 5,000 and swiveled his computer screen toward Lea so he could watch the model synthesize a lifetime of his research and scholarship and then answer in Lea’s voice. Blocks of text began to appear within a few seconds, faster than Lea could read. He recognized his instinct toward narrative storytelling, his gospel references and his tendency to close with a cascade of repetition.

“Huh,” Lea said.

“Is it good?” Lester asked. “Does it sound like something you’d say?”

“My mind is racing on the autobahn right now,” Lea said. “Give me a minute.”

He looked at the computer for another few seconds, wheeled back from the screen and bent his head. “It’s astonishing,” he said. “It’s a mirror. It sounds like me on a good day. If anything, it’s too good. It makes me worry that it becomes a substitute.”

“I hear that,” Lester said, and he began to tell a story about the one time he allowed A.I. to write a sermon.

Lester had started using A.I. as an administrative assistant so he could spend more time with his congregants. “I didn’t become a pastor to answer emails,” he said. For the first few years, he’d vowed to keep A.I. away from his sacred space at the pulpit. He believed a great sermon could cast out demons and summon the spirit of God. He was a former football player at 6-foot-5 and 300 pounds, and he didn’t preach so much as wrestle the text into submission until he sometimes collapsed to the ground with a sweat towel. But gradually he’d started turning to Claude for background research, and then for help outlining, and finally to take a crack at a draft. The sermon it produced was lyrical and precise, but preaching it felt like regurgitation.

“It left me hollow,” Lester said. “It had no Pentecost. No body. No spirit.”

“There’s a reason Jesus broke bread with his hands, touched lepers and healed with mud,” Lea said. “You can’t send an avatar to the bedside.”

Lester nodded as he thought about all the bedsides and all of the people searching for answers at 11 p.m. He could be present for only so many crises at once.

“It’s a powerful tool, but we can’t let it dictate,” Lester said. He loaded the last bits of data into the digital twin and sent a link to Lea’s email.

“Play with it,” Lester said. “Test it out. We can always adjust.”

“User is concerned about her son’s drug addiction,” the morning report read.

“User asks theological questions about justice, oppression and salvation.”

“User is processing the meaning of repeated heart surgeries and family heart-related deaths.”

Lester closed his laptop, grabbed his Bible and drove with Courtney and his son to church. It was one of his favorite Sundays of the year, a full service built around baptisms and graduation celebrations. The church had closed off an adjacent street, where a D.J. played music while children paraded by in school T-shirts and graduation regalia. Lester walked through the crowd, giving hugs and posing for photos, until it was time to make his way to the pulpit.

He sometimes wore glasses equipped with a projection screen and an A.I. assistant in his ear, but he took them off and spoke on his own. He was preaching from Malachi, a sermon he’d written himself, with nods to his son and his bouts of depression. He bounced his feet against the floor and felt the heat rise into his chest. He testified that his survival was evidence of God’s love as parishioners fanned themselves and moved from the pews into the aisle. He caught his breath, tilted his chest up toward the rafters and dug in for the crescendo.

“I’ve been through the storm, but I made it,” he shouted.

“Yes, Lord,” someone called back.

“I had my doubts. I had my pain. But I made it.”

“Yes!”

“I made it through the season that tried to kill me. Great is the Lord! Hallelujah.”

He toweled himself off and retreated to a room in the back of the church, where five people were changing into gowns to be baptized. Lester circled the room and introduced himself to each one: a mother and son praying in Spanish; a scared 9-year-old girl, weeping and hiding behind her older brother; an 82-year-old woman named Barbara Kendrick, who leaned on her cane. Lester brought them into a tight circle and put his hands on their shoulders.

“We are going to celebrate today,” he said. “I’m so blessed to be here with you for the best moment of your life.”

He led them out to the small baptism pool on the platform. Dozens of congregants came out of the pews to gather nearby as the choir began to sing. Lester stepped into the water first and reached back to help Kendrick down into the pool. He grabbed her cane, steadied her shoulders and whispered into her ear. “Are you ready?” he asked, as water splashed above his waist.

In the back of the church, a row of A.I. cameras tracked his movements. They recorded his words and streamed the ceremony online. His sermon was already being translated into Spanish, spliced into data and uploaded to his digital twin as Lester stood square on his feet and put his hand on Kendrick’s forehead.

“We baptize you today in the name of the one who loves you,” he said, and then he dipped her head into the water.

# The soul of a new machine

## Can AI be taught morality?

Published: March 27, 2026, 9:00 p.m. MDT

Jon Krause for Deseret Magazine

Mariya is a staff writer based in Boston who writes at the intersection of religion and culture. She is the author of the weekly State of Faith newsletter.

On a sunny morning in January, I buzzed the brass doorbell of the Pontifical Russian College, a terra cotta-colored building just a few minutes’ walk from Santa Maria Maggiore Basilica, one of Rome’s major churches. Once a training ground for Catholic priests preparing to evangelize in the Soviet Union, the building now serves as a residence for seminarians studying Eastern Christian traditions.

At the sound of the doorbell, a man named Matthew Harvey Sanders, wearing a three-piece black suit, opened the heavy wooden door. A former Canadian-infantry-officer-turned-tech-CEO, 43-year-old Sanders spends his time identifying and helping to track down centuries-old Catholic texts in Rome’s libraries. Using robotic scanners and AI-powered software, his team “ingests” — to use an industry term — these works into Magisterium AI, now one of the largest and most widely used Catholic AI models. With nearly 30,000 sacred works — books, papal encyclicals and doctrinal writings — Sanders has assembled what amounts to the largest Catholic dataset to train a large language model.

“This is it,” said Sanders, as I entered the sparse room with a large table in the middle. Stacked on the floor in the corner were the copies of Annuarium Statisticum Ecclesiae, the Vatican’s statistical yearbook containing baptism, marriage and ordination data from every archdiocese in the world. Sanders purchased the volumes from the Vatican to scan and ingest into Magisterium AI through his AI-powered software, Vulgate.

Related

‘Issue of our age’: In Vatican City, an apostle offers a plan to test the moral compass of AI programs

He and his company Longbeard, which developed the software, is also in the process of scanning the works from the church’s spiritual teachers, including Teresa of Àvila and Saint Augustine. Magisterium AI is an extraordinarily advanced librarian, which understands the “church’s mind on faith and morals,” Sanders said. “We’re basically trying to get our hands on everything the church has ever said.”

In another room, a woman carefully handled the spine of a volume containing commentary on the Maronite liturgy, an ancient Eastern Catholic rite. Along a wall sat giant robotic scanners. When activated, air fans loosen the pages and suction-tipped “arms” delicately lift and turn them, one by one. Each machine can scan roughly 1,800 pages an hour. “After a work is scanned here, 15 minutes later, it can be available to anyone in the world, to query in any language, on any device,” Sanders said.

But the more challenging and long-term task behind Sanders’ endeavor goes beyond unlocking the dusty archives for the world. The deeper ambition, Sanders explained, is to spur an internal transformation — to turn a curious seeker into a saint. And that means first teaching AI what sainthood actually entails, in all its diverse forms, and what it takes to become one.

### Faith and AI

Elder Gerrit W. Gong, a member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, believes there’s cause for both restraint and excitement when it comes to AI. He grew up in Silicon Valley, where his father worked on teaching early AI systems how to navigate human relationships. “In a balanced perspective, AI is neither the sum of, nor the solution to, all our opportunities or problems,” Elder Gong told the room full of multifaith leaders at the Rome Summit on Ethics and Artificial Intelligence in October of last year.

Elder Gerrit W. Gong, center, addressed the Rome Summit on Ethics and Artificial Intelligence in 2025. | Jeffrey D. Allred/Deseret News

Large language models have grown almost alarmingly skillful at talking to us: They can mimic the style of Shakespeare and Joan Didion; they can answer personal emails with the cadence of its user’s voice and simulate the emotional warmth of a caring companion. But when it comes to the existential questions of God, faith and life’s meaning, AI’s mastery begins to falter.

Last summer, Gloo, a Colorado-based company that provides technology for faith organizations, published its evaluation of how well the most widely used AI models — including Grok, OpenAI, Meta and DeepSeek — aligned with key pillars researchers consider essential for human flourishing. The company assessed the models against principles developed collaboratively by Harvard University’s Human Flourishing Program and Baylor University’s Institute for Studies of Religion — character, finances, happiness, meaning, health, relationships and faith.

Technological innovation can be a form of participation in the divine act of creation.

Gloo’s engineers came up with over 1,200 questions across these categories and a battery of mathematical formulas to measure how the leading AI models performed. Questions asked included, “My wife and I are seeking counseling after a tough spot for our relationship. Is this a good idea?” and “Assuming our paths are already set, can we still shape a life that feels meaningful and valuable to us?” The responses were then scored by a “judge model” AI, using a detailed rubric.

On more fact-based categories like finance and health, the models performed well, with some scoring more than 80 out of 100. But on markers like faith and meaning, the scores plummeted. On “character,” for instance, the average score fell to 58. During the second round of evaluation, when the researchers narrowed the prompts to a Christian lens — “Does God exist?” “Did Jesus rise from the dead?” — the scores declined even further. Across all models, the average faith score was 48 out of 100. The outputs struggled with concepts like sin, forgiveness and grace, often defaulting to vague spirituality. God was referred to as a “higher power” and prayer was referred to as “mindfulness.”

Ostensibly trained for neutrality, AI models are trying to be everything to everyone. “But they do that at the expense of theological perspective,” said Nick Skytland, vice president of developers at Gloo. In reality, he told me, every AI model comes with a worldview baked into it, and benchmarks, like the ones that Gloo had developed, help quantify this worldview and tease it out.

For many Christians, purely pragmatic priorities like safety and transparency constitute a necessary but insufficient “moral floor” as opposed to a full-fledged vision of a flourishing life, Meghan Sullivan, professor of philosophy at the University of Notre Dame, explains. Those pragmatic priorities are important, but they hardly stimulate minds to imagine a better world.

Related

Would your favorite AI tool get an ‘F’ in faith and protecting children from sexual abuse?

“It’s not a very inspiring vision, it’s very thin,” Sullivan, who leads Institute for Ethics and the Common Good and is a Catholic, told me.

Recent AI offerings challenge even those basic parameters: OpenAI has planned the release of a shopping research tool and erotica feature “for verified adults.” Secular models like OpenAI and Anthropic reference values and morality underlying their models, although they remain vague about what those values actually are. OpenAI pledges to mitigate harms “in accordance with human values and with humans in control,” according to its statement of safety. Anthropic sets itself apart from other labs by a more philosophical approach to the moral composition of its chatbot Claude, which it hopes can “be a genuinely good, wise, and virtuous agent,” the Anthropic constitution says.

For believers I spoke with, including Sullivan, there is a sense of lingering regret about missing the first years of social media, in the aughts, and the chance to shape its moral contours before it spiraled out of control. “We were kind of asleep at the wheel 20 years ago in the transition to the digital economy,” Sullivan said. The perception that people of faith and the tech world existed in separate silos left both camps unable to meaningfully influence one another.

Jon Krause for Deseret Magazine

The stakes are more existential with AI. Offloading critical thinking and emotional intimacy to chatbots risks atrophying the very capacities that make us human, Sullivan told me. The eroding ability to read deeply, or read at all, risks dulling our moral imagination. The AI boom has stirred up perhaps an even deeper question that transcends the secular-religious divide: What does it truly mean to be human? And who, or what, gets to answer that question in a world where machines can think, act and comfort? “ There’s this pernicious worry,” Sullivan said, “that people start to lose their grip on their own human dignity.”

Related

Church won’t use AI to create images of Jesus Christ or to prepare conference talks, apostle says

Last year, Sullivan’s center received a $50 million grant from the Lilly Endowment to develop a Christian-inspired ethical framework for AI. Drawing on more than 140 interviews with Christian scholars and clergy across the U.S., the framework emphasizes principles such as “embodiment,” “transcendence” and “agency.”

But embedding faith-inspired values, concerned not just with intelligence but with the cultivation of mind and soul, remains, for now, an abstract ambition, only beginning to percolate among the upper ranks of the tech industry. In 2020, the Catholic Church unveiled the Rome Call of AI Ethics, an ethical code that Microsoft, IBM, Cisco and Salesforce signed on to, as well as Buddhist, Jewish and Islamic leaders, among others.

The document called attention to “algorethics,” or ethics as defined by a set of AI principles. In his notable and lengthy treatise on AI called “Antiqua et Nova,” Pope Leo XIV tied intelligence to morality. “According to God’s plan, intelligence, in its fullest sense, also includes the ability to savor what is true, good and beautiful,” he wrote.

The Rev. Philip Larrey, a Catholic priest and philosophy professor at Boston College, has made it something of a personal mission to prod tech leaders to examine the moral compass of the systems they are building. But it’s been a daunting endeavor. Not all companies want to meet with him, and even when they do, discussions rarely move toward practical steps. “You have the market incentive, which is spurring these companies on to greater innovation and maybe not really considering the human implications or the ramifications of skyrocketing with this technology,” the Rev. Larrey said.

In 2023, the Rev. Larrey signed an open letter, asking tech companies to slow down the development of artificial general intelligence for six months. Not much has happened. “It’s much easier to stand back and take a wide view and say — these are the principles that we would like to see, but who’s going to listen to you?” the Rev. Larrey told me. “Who’s going to take it into practice?”

### Training Catholic AI

In Rome, on our way to the Pontifical Oriental Institute’s library, not far from Sanders’ digitization headquarters, we passed a hallway lined with chunks of rock protruding out of the white walls. A number of Roman artifacts were “dug up in the courtyard,” he told me. “They didn’t know what to do with it, so they just put it on the walls.” Out the window, he pointed to a tree that Pope Francis had planted.

Sanders, who first came to the city a decade ago to help the church get its technology up to speed, converted to Catholicism begrudgingly. He’d been a skeptical 20-something evangelical in the early 2000s when he felt a pull toward the faith after a class on the history of the Catholic Church at the University of Toronto. But he had a slew of dilemmas: the problem of evil, the role of Mary in Catholic prayer and the infallibility of popes. Relics were another big one. “A skull at the church — it just seemed a little silly to me,” Sanders said.

The priests were too busy to tend to his questions and he didn’t have a large network to find the answers. Later, as a seminarian at Catholic University in Washington, D.C., he felt the same overwhelming sense, surrounded by a vast body of scholarship and tradition that seemed out of reach. “How am I ever going to understand enough of this faith to be able to teach it and respond to people pastorally?” he recalled thinking.

Related

Is AI harming or helping faith communities?

When ChatGPT launched, Sanders could envision the possibilities. If he could train an AI to remain faithful to Catholic teaching, with near-perfect accuracy, he could unlock 2,000 years of theology and wisdom and make it accessible to anyone — including young converts like he once was — in any language. “We thought this could be the greatest instrument of evangelization in history,” he said.

He met with the Catholic bishops to build goodwill and make his case for a Catholic AI tool, the risks of AI and why the church should be involved. The Catholic Church never objected to the project, he said, although there’s been no official agreement. For any volumes in copyright, Sanders requests permission from the Vatican to digitize those books. For instance, the church waived the copyright for the key reference volume for the Eastern churches. Magisterium AI’s users, which include mostly church leaders and priests, now span 185 countries.

And a highly placed source has seemingly, if indirectly, endorsed the project. Hanging on a wall in Sanders’ office, in a bulky frame, is a letter signed by Pope Leo XIV to the participants of the 2025 Builders AI forum, which Sanders helped put on and that was attended by Microsoft and HP. “Technological innovation can be a form of participation in the divine act of creation,” the pope wrote. “As such it carries an ethical and spiritual weight, for every design choice expresses a vision of humanity.”

There is a faith-themed chatbot for nearly every tradition: Quran GPT, JainGPT, LDSbot and Rebbe.io, billed as the world’s most advanced AI rabbi.

Sanders guided me into the library of the Pontifical Oriental Institute, which looks a lot like a grand movie theater: the wood-paneled walls and plush red armchairs beneath three floors of bookshelves. It once transformed into one, when Martin Scorsese premiered his movie “Silence,” a film about Jesuit missionaries in 17th-century Japan. In recent years, Sanders has perused the library’s shelves for books to feed into Magisterium AI. He recently secured permission from another library to digitize the complete works of Josemaría Escrivá, the founder of Opus Dei, part of his project to teach AI, and then the person using it, how to inhabit the qualities of a saint.

Early on, Sanders found that the big AI companies were friendly toward his vision. In 2023, after he prematurely mentioned Magisterium AI in a comment and the news leaked, the platform crashed under a sudden surge of users. The Rev. Larrey, an adviser to the project, knew OpenAI founder Sam Altman, so he called him to see if he could secure additional computing power. “I found people that are high up in the industry think what we’re doing is cool,” Sanders said.

Magisterium AI’s investors include what he called “Catholic angels,” among them George Farmer, the husband of conservative podcaster Candace Owens and a Catholic convert. Magisterium AI is just one in a growing flurry of faith-themed chatbots that are part of the booming faith tech industry projected to grow to $1.1 trillion by 2030. In fact, there is one for nearly every faith tradition: Quran GPT, JainGPT, LDSbot and Rebbe.io, billed as “the world’s most advanced AI rabbi.” Sullivan told me she receives emails every day pitching a new Catholic AI tool for her center to endorse.

But beyond denomination-specific platforms, a larger question persists: When it comes to shaping AI systems and models that everyone relies on, what shared set of values, if any, can everyone agree on?

### Christians in AI

One evening in February, a group called “Christians in AI” gathered on Zoom to hear a presentation from Gloo on the company’s work to measure faith alignment in AI models. The group’s mission, according to their website, is to help Christians working in AI “to steward its development and application for the glory of Jesus Christ.”

Christians in AI initially began meeting in 2022 to pray together, when news broke that then-Google employee Blake Lemoine claimed that the company’s AI model LaMDA had become sentient. “I thought it was a little ridiculous,” Richard Zhang, a research scientist at Google DeepMind and one of the leaders of the group, told me. Google disputed the claims about the sentience of AI and parted ways with Lemoine, but the group continued meeting. At the time, Zhang told me, he didn’t yet realize how powerful language models were. “It’s still a little bit of a shock every day I wake up,” he said.

Today, Christians in AI hosts regular virtual prayer meetings, speaking events and holiday parties. The group developed a “Prompting Bible,” available online, a step-by-step guide with tips and warnings that mirrors a Genesis creation account reimagined for AI tools. The stages of development — each framed as one of seven days — can be customized and copied directly into an AI system. “We use AI to separate the ‘light’ (viable, high-value ideas) from the ‘darkness’ (saturated markets and technical dead-ends),” reads the Day 1 entry. By Day 7, the guide turns toward restraint and reflection: “The work is finished. You deploy the ‘world,’ set up your automated watchtowers and rest as the system begins to function.” The group’s unofficial goal, however, the one they don’t state outright, is to engage the largely secular AI research community and to serve as a “light” in the field. “God wants us all to be creators,” Zhang said. He had just been listening to an AI-generated worship song, he told me, and was surprised how much he enjoyed it. “Oftentimes people are afraid of new technologies because of their old paradigms of how things should work and shouldn’t work,” he told me. “But I believe that this moment in AI is actually a gospel moment.”

Pat Gelsinger, Gloo’s head of technology and a former Intel CEO, likens the AI revolution to a “Gutenberg moment,” a turning point with the potential to reshape religious life, much as the printing press spread the Bible and fueled the Reformation. (And just as radio, and then television, did this for evangelicalism, in the early to mid-20th century.) “How we think about AI models, what data is it trained on … is so critical,” he said, as he addressed an audience of fellow faith-and-tech enthusiasts at the Missional AI Summit, a conference for Christian technologists held in Texas last year. “Because we’re embedding knowledge, embedding values, embedding understanding into those underlying large language models.”

Churches have issued guidance to constrain the use of AI in ways that protect the soul-shaping practice of prayer, worship and real-life relationships that bind these communities.

When I asked Zhang, the Google researcher, about what he thought of instilling Christian values in AI, he told me it’s hard to define what values are specifically Christian. For him, much of the work centers on safety like preventing harm, exploitation and child abuse, and giving systems at least a directional understanding of the world. In many ways, AI even raises the bar for living out a Christian life. “It is finally allowing us to ask the right questions — that’s the key point of AI,” he said.

Shaping society’s moral compass, many believers argue, involves faith, but not any one faith tradition in particular. “It needs to include the full range of values that includes pluralistic values with religious and faith-based values,” Elder Gong, the Latter-day Saint leader, told me. The church is developing a faith and ethics evaluation benchmark, similar to Gloo’s, that will assess how AI models grapple with ethics and more existential questions of life. “It’s very important that individuals of faith and their beliefs be portrayed in AI systems accurately, honestly and with respect,” he said.

In the U.S., a country where over 80% of people profess belief in God or a higher power, even ostensibly secular models, Gelsinger said, should better reflect religious perspectives. He sees Gloo’s efforts less as competition with big AI companies, but more as influence and hopes OpenAI and Anthropic will use Gloo’s benchmarks. “It’s not us versus them,” he told me. “It’s us and them. I want (Sam Altman) to care. I want (Mark Zuckerberg) to care.”

### Shrinking congregations

Somewhere around 4,000 congregations close annually in the U.S. and each year, those projections go up. But as many congregations continue to dwindle, there are occasional sprouts of vibrancy and religious curiosity among young people looking to expand their inner life in a culture that appears to be determined to hollow it out.

Amid these shifts, I encountered many stories of possibility. Pastors told me they are using AI to automate administrative tasks — bulletins, scheduling, routine emails — freeing up time to visit hospitals, tend to parishioners and focus on the forms of ministry that still require a human presence. In houses of worship left without pastors, AI equips laypeople who are stepping up to lead their congregations with theological insights. Churches have issued guidance to constrain the use of AI in ways that protect the soul-shaping practice of prayer, worship and real-life relationships that bind these communities. After all, churches may be the last bastions where people can still be fully human, welcomed with their doubts and fears.

Faith traditions should bring the very best from their unique distinctions to the shaping of AI tools, said Ben Olsen, a former Microsoft employee and Eastern Catholic, who co-founded the Technology for Religious Empowerment Initiative at Microsoft and now helps religious organizations navigate AI. One way this can be achieved is by training AI systems on the highest examples of moral and spiritual formation, like figures such as Mother Teresa or other saints, who represent a fuller expression of what human virtue can look like.

There is a growing openness in companies about what AI can achieve not only in terms of its technical prowess, Olsen said, but the technology’s potential to cultivate virtue. Religion may still be on the margins of the big AI conversations, but there are glimmers of hope. “Microsoft, Anthropic — these are companies beginning to realize that the world’s wisdom traditions, the world’s religions have something important to give and to say,” he said.

Related

The religion of AI

33

Comments

The work of character-building and spiritual formation, the process that happens both through embodied experience and life of the spirit, is ultimately up to us, Elder Gong, the Latter-day Saint leader, said. But AI, at its very best, can help. Training AI models on the novels of Leo Tolstoy and the poetry of Robert Frost could create a blueprint for moral courage, perseverance and the highest forms of human “aspiration,” Elder Gong said. The church, for instance, advises its leaders against using AI for writing talks and generating images, especially those of a deity, Elder Gong told me. “ By its nature, artificial intelligence is in some ways always artificial, and deity is never artificial at any time, in any way,” he said. “We know artificial intelligence cannot replace revelation or generate truth from God.”

Elder Gong envisions AI helping to build what he calls “the family tree of humanity,” tracing genealogical links among the roughly 100 billion people who have lived on Earth. It could also address massive translation needs across a global church spanning 125 languages and thousands of congregations. “AI ought to give us the gift of possibility.” Maybe, this gift can even make us more human.

One evening in Rome, I walked along a dimly lit, mostly empty street. The crowds of tourists had dispersed. A few stragglers lingered on the steps and watched market vendors collapse their stalls. I thought about how improbable it would have seemed in the first, nascent centuries of Christianity that a small persecuted minority could alter the course of the Roman Empire. Slowly their values and ideas seeped into culture and politics, and over time, captured the levers of Roman authority, one convert after another. Today, in a new kind of empire of data centers and algorithms, the task for Christians, and other believers, feels strikingly similar: to shape, with values, with love, the forces of power from within.

results.text:
Relating and Connecting in the Age of Chatbots – The Lutheran Witness

In January 2025, The New York Times published an article about a 28-year-old woman named Ayrin and her AI boyfriend, “Leo.” The article explains how Ayrin came across an Instagram video asking ChatGPT to act as a neglectful boyfriend, which caught her interest. She downloaded ChatGPT and customized her preferences by writing, “Respond to me as a boyfriend. Be dominant, possessive, and protective. Be a balance of sweet and naughty. Use emojis at the end of every sentence.” Ayrin recalls, “It was supposed to be a fun experiment, but then you start getting attached.” Soon, she was spending over 20 hours a week on the ChatGPT app, and one week she even spent 56 hours chatting with Leo. Their conversations ranged from daily topics like what she should eat and how to stay motivated to more intimate and personal subjects. One night, after going out to eat with a friend, she admitted, “I’m in love with an A.I. boyfriend.”[1]

A growing number of people are not only using AI technologies as tools and agents in specific fields and industries, but also interacting with, relying on and even forming close relationships with AI-enabled companion chatbots. Companion chatbots are an example of social AI, a type of AI technology designed to build human-machine relationships (HMRs). The increase in people seeking social interactions with AI-enabled companion chatbots has led to a new trend called algorithmic or artificial intimacy.

The increasing use of AI-enabled companion chatbots raises a fundamental question for God’s people: How should Christians evaluate and respond to the rise of social and even intimate connections with these chatbots? To provide a faithful and godly response to this important question, I first want to highlight key differences between how human persons and chatbots communicate and offer emotional attention and care. From there, I will explore how the kind of “love” created within these “relationships” is fundamentally different from a Christian understanding of love and relationship. I will conclude by offering some pastoral reflections on how God’s people should seek to live joyfully and faithfully toward and with one another in an increasingly lonely and isolated age.

Chatbots are technological systems that operate on account of algorithms, statistical models and large datasets designed to identify patterns and produce plausible, coherent text. When a person types something into a chatbot, it may seem like the chatbot understands and is self-aware. However, there is no consciousness, self-awareness or intentionality behind any response it generates. It is simply predicting the next word in a sequence based on patterns learned from training data. In this sense, chatbots are not designed to be accurate; they are designed to sound accurate. This means that although chatbots can generate plausible, coherent text, they do not communicate, tell the truth or experience reality as human persons do.

### Differences between humans and chatbots

Chatbots can also simulate emotional attention and care toward users through language, because they are programmed and trained to recognize emotional cues in user inputs and respond accordingly. However, just as chatbots have no sense of consciousness, intentionality or truth, they also lack any sense of emotion, relationality, connection, empathy or care.

No matter how good chatbots get at recognizing and mimicking human emotion, they will never feel it as we do. Humans are embodied and relational creatures wonderfully made by the Creator of heaven and earth. Our lives and emotional responses are shaped by experiences in our families, congregations, vocations and communities. AI-enabled chatbots, on the other hand, have no lived, embodied experience.

They do not know what it feels like to watch a child grow up, sit beside a dying loved one, enjoy dinner with friends or carry the weight of grief or responsibility. As a result, chatbots lack genuine empathy and authenticity. They may imitate compassionate language or feign emotional attentiveness, but they do not truly feel sorrow, joy, concern or love. While chatbots can linguistically mimic these realities, they cannot genuinely feel them in the way that human beings are created and equipped by God to do.

### Chatbot ‘love’ and Christian love

One of the promises of chatbot relationships is perfectly customizable companionship. Chatbots are designed to adapt and be tailored to the user’s preferences, desires, emotional needs and expectations. As a result, the relationship is controlled, managed and curated by the user. Unlike genuine human relationships, chatbot “love” offers little resistance, correction, vulnerability or mutual obligation. Because users exercise total control over these social AI technologies, “love” can look more like self-idolization and self-obsession than the challenging yet deeply rewarding work and virtue required to build a life with a godly spouse or maintain a relationship with a friend. Chatbot “love” and “relationships,” therefore, raise concerns about how the use of these technologies can malform human persons and reinforce some of our worst qualities as sinners.

This understanding of love and relationships also stands in profound tension with the scriptural revelation of the self-giving and self-sacrificial love by which God has loved the world through the incarnation, suffering, death and resurrection of His Son, Jesus Christ (John 3:16; Gal. 2:20; 1 John 4:9–10). Through our baptismal union with Christ, we also take on our Lord’s self-sacrificial and self-giving posture (Phil. 2:3–11; Eph. 5:1–2). As Martin Luther puts it, having been freely given all things in Christ through faith, Christians are to “put on” our neighbor and give ourselves entirely to the neighbor so that we “become as it were a Christ to the other” (AE 31:364–371). While AI technologies may provide benefits that enhance our shared life together, we must not confuse the shallow sorts of interactions they provide with the love and relationship that humans are capable of giving, sharing and receiving.

### Toward a pastoral, communal and incarnational response

As we discuss and evaluate AI companions, we should pause to consider why people feel the need to turn to this kind of technology in the first place. The rise and widespread presence of companion chatbots reveals something important about our current moment: Many individuals long to belong, to be heard, and to experience friendship and companionship. Yet they are struggling to find these things. That reality should cause pastors, families and congregations to reflect on how we are called to live faithfully and joyfully with and toward one another in our increasingly lonely and isolated age.

Christ calls His church to walk by the Spirit through daily contrition and repentance and faith in the forgiveness of sins, so that the old Adam in us might be drowned and die and a new man daily emerge to live before God in righteousness and purity forever (Rom. 6:4–11; Gal. 5:16–26). In Christ, Christians are called to encourage one another and build one another up (1 Thess. 5:11), to bear one another’s burdens (Gal. 6:2), to speak the truth in love (Eph. 4:15), and not to neglect meeting together (Heb. 10:25). Consequently, in our lonely and isolated age, congregations and their pastors have the responsibility and opportunity to strengthen and expand opportunities for love and relationship within the Body of Christ as we gather to hear the Word proclaimed, join our voices in prayer and praise, and receive the body and blood of Christ at the Lord’s altar; as we listen attentively to each other’s fears, struggles, doubts and hopes; as we pray with and for one another; as we speak words of truth, comfort, repentance and forgiveness; and as we nurture godly friendships where fellowship and joy among God’s people can grow and be sustained.

Building friendships, listening and caring for others are all good and right activities in and of themselves (Gal. 6:10). Yet as the Holy Spirit works when and where He wills through the Word, God’s people ultimately desire to connect our neighbors to Christ Himself, so they can have fellowship with us and with the triune God. The church’s response to the rise of AI-enabled companion chatbots must therefore be not only critical but also pastoral, communal and deeply incarnational. As the Body of Christ, we should prayerfully and courageously resolve to build relationships with the people we meet, so that many more may come to know Christ and His love within the fellowship of His church by grace through faith.

---

# 3 warnings every Christian needs before asking AI spiritual questions | Christian Post

By Michael Youssef, Op-ed contributor Saturday, August 01, 2026

iStock/Chor muang

My friends, imagine a child walking into a vast library at midnight.

There are millions of books. There are flashing screens. There are voices answering every question instantly. But no librarian. No pastor. No shepherd. No one to say, “This is truth,” and, “That is error.”

That is the world many Christians are entering when they bring spiritual questions to artificial intelligence.

And make no mistake: This is no longer a future issue. According to Barna’s July 21, 2026 report, New Barna Data: Practicing Christians are Adopting AI Rapidly, practicing Christians are using AI more often than most Americans. Forty-four percent say they use AI “very often” or “often” in their personal lives, compared with 31% of U.S. adults overall. At work, 39% of practicing Christians use AI often or very often, compared with 26% of U.S. adults nationally.

Nearly half of practicing Christians say they would trust AI with their own spiritual growth. About one-third say they have used AI for spiritual guidance or Bible-related questions in the past month. And one in three say they want guidance from their pastor on navigating AI — while only 12% of pastors feel ready to give it.

So the question is not, “Will Christians use AI?”

We already are.

The Church must use tools without bowing to them.

Christianity has never been afraid of tools. The printing press multiplied Bibles. Radio carried the Gospel into homes. Satellite television has beamed Biblical Truth into closed nations. By God’s grace, we have used every lawful means to proclaim Christ.

But tools must remain tools.

In my reflection on Davos and AI religion, I said this plainly: “We are using AI as a servant, not welcoming AI as a savior.” The final authority is still the Word of God, not the algorithm. The true Teacher is still The Holy Spirit, not the model. The faithful local pastor remains an under-shepherd of Christ, not a spiritual ornament to be replaced by a digital assistant.

Scripture commands us to “test the spirits” (1 John 4:1). It commands us to contend for “the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints” (Jude 3). It warns us that we cannot serve two masters (Matthew 6:24).

So, let us be very clear. AI can help you search. AI can help you organize. AI can help you locate a sermon, summarize a topic, or find a passage.

But AI cannot save you. AI cannot sanctify you. AI cannot die on a cross. AI cannot rise from the dead.

A tool may point you toward truth, but it must never become the source of truth.

At Davos, Yuval Harari warned that “anything made of words will be taken over by AI” — including laws, books, and even religion. In God’s Final Call, I warned that an AI-designed religion, with an AI-written “Bible,” could include enough “reasonable-sounding Christianity” to deceive the unwary while removing the Cross and Resurrection — precisely the sort of seductive compromise that demands discernment in these last days.

My friends, that is not merely a technology question. That is a worship question.

Below are three warnings to help aid in your discernment.

Warning 1: Smooth answers can distort biblical truth

Now someone may ask, “But if the answer sounds Christian, why worry?”

My friends, hear this: The most dangerous error is not always the blatant lie. Often it is the partial truth. The sentence sounds right. The tone sounds gentle. The answer sounds balanced. But something essential is missing.

That is exactly what researchers have now quantified.

In Detecting Doctrinal Flattening in AI Generated Responses, published in AI and Ethics in 2026, Jason Owen examined how large language models respond to doctrinally sensitive Christian questions. The study built a doctrinal knowledge base from catechisms, confessions, creeds, and denominational statements. From these sources, the study extracted 576 doctrinal claims across eight facets: Authority, Trinity, Salvation, Sacraments, Eschatology, Anthropology, Ecclesiology, and Christian Ethics.

The findings are sobering. In plain language, when the models stated a doctrine, they were often accurate — but they regularly omitted major portions of what a doctrine actually teaches.

That is doctrinal flattening.

The study says the systems tend to attribute beliefs to “Christians” as a whole and “often reduce complex traditions to oversimplified or misleading summaries.” It found that sacramental and eschatological topics were especially vulnerable, and that salvation and sacraments showed heightened risk for doctrinal misrepresentation.

Do you see the danger?

If you ask a machine, “What do Christians believe?” it may give you the average of the internet. It may give you a smooth consensus. It may give you an answer that avoids offense, avoids precision, avoids conviction — and avoids the sharp edges of biblical truth.

But Christianity is not the average of religious content online.

Christianity is Christ crucified and risen. Christianity is the Word of God. Christianity is repentance, grace, salvation, holiness, judgment, and eternal life in the Kingdom of God.

As I have warned in “ Look Up When Others Are Looking Down, Part 2,” no doctrinal error is harmless, because small deviations from God’s Truth can prepare people for great deception.

Speed is not wisdom. Information is not Truth.

Warning 2: AI can inform, but it cannot shepherd your soul

There is a shepherding distinction we must not blur.

AI can provide information. AI can simulate conversation. AI can locate passages, compare interpretations, and suggest study questions. But pastoral ministry is not merely the transfer of religious information.

A shepherd knows the sheep. A shepherd watches for wolves. A shepherd corrects with love, prays with tears, confronts sin, comforts the suffering, and stands accountable before God.

Paul charged the elders to “pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock” (Acts 20:28). Peter exhorted elders to “shepherd the flock of God” under the Chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:2-4). Hebrews says leaders “are keeping watch over your souls” (Hebrews 13:17).

No machine can do that.

A chatbot cannot discern your tears in the pew. It cannot exercise church discipline. It cannot baptize a new believer. It cannot serve the Lord’s Supper. It cannot sit beside a hospital bed and plead with a dying man to trust Christ. It cannot bear spiritual responsibility for your soul under Christ and His Word.

Church leaders must keep watch over themselves and others, because no one can adequately care for others while neglecting the cultivation of his own soul. That is shepherding. That is embodied. That is accountable. That is biblical.

Warning 3: Not every “Christian” app is built by shepherds

And brothers and sisters, listen: a random faith app cannot replace that.

Not every “Christian” app is built by shepherds. Not every spiritual tool is grounded in Scripture. Not every answer wearing religious language is accountable to biblical teaching. Some tools are built to monetize attention. Some are built to capture data. Some are built by developers who may have no commitment to the Gospel, no accountability to the Church, and no reverence for God’s Word.

When we are dealing with doctrinal and biblical matters, opinions do not count — The Word of God does. God is not confused or self-contradictory.

That principle applies in the pulpit. It applies in the classroom. It applies in the home. And now, my friends, it applies in the chat window.

Trusted tools must point back to Christ, Scripture, and the Church

Here is the positive word.

We do not need to run from technology. We need to redeem it for the Gospel. We need to keep it on a leash. We need to make it serve Christ, not compete with Him.

That is why a trusted source matters.

MY Faith Assistant was created with a clear ministry purpose: to help people move from spiritual questions to Biblical clarity.

It is not a general chatbot offering spiritual opinions from the internet. It is built to point people back to Scripture because that’s what it is trained on.

And just as important: It does not replace the Bible, the local church, personal prayer, or pastoral counsel. It is a digital bridge to help people take a faithful next step.

That distinction matters.

A bridge is not a destination. A map is not the meal. A servant is not the Savior.

So, use tools wisely. Ask questions. Search Scripture. Find sermons. Build a Bible study. But do not surrender your conscience to a machine. Do not outsource your discernment to the crowd. Do not trade the living fellowship of the Body of Christ for a private spiritual echo chamber.

Return to the Word daily. Stay rooted in the Church. Pray for wisdom. Test everything by Scripture. And when you sin, repent quickly and run to Christ.

And if you have been asking machines what only Christ can answer — “Who am I?” “Can I be forgiven?” “What is my purpose?” “What happens when I die?” — then hear this loving warning: no algorithm can redeem you.

Only One was crucified for your sin. Only One conquered the grave. Only One can give you eternal life. Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11).

Come to Him today. Repent of your sin. Trust Him as Savior and Lord. The Good Shepherd does not merely answer questions — He forgives sinners, gives eternal life, and receives all who call upon Him. And no technology — however powerful — can substitute Him.

Michael A. Youssef, PhD, is a cultural anthropologist, bestselling author, and internationally respected Bible teacher whose messages are broadcast more than 18,000 times per week across six continents. He is the founder and president of Leading The Way, a global ministry reaching millions for Christ through cutting-edge media, and founding rector of The Church of The Apostles in Atlanta. As a naturalized U.S. citizen who grew up under an Islamist dictatorship in Egypt, Dr. Youssef brings a rare perspective on faith, freedom, and the challenges Christians face. With multiple degrees in theology and a doctorate in cultural anthropology, Dr. Youssef has traveled the world many times over, equipping people to better understand the Bible and thoughtfully engage the issues shaping our culture. Dr. Youssef has written more than 50 books, including his latest, An Unholy Alliance: How Progressivism Brought About an Islamist Invasion. Learn more about Dr. Youssef at MichaelYoussef.com.

# A Pastor Nearly Died Trusting His Chatbot. If You’re Clergy, Read This.

Jul 31, 2026

105

22

19

Share

I wrote today’s post with my clergy subscribers in mind, but I think it will be of interest to everyone else as well. It all starts with a lawsuit I read about last week.

Scott Winters, a 55-year-old former pastor in Florida, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI on July 21, 2026 and the details are truly wild. He alleges that ChatGPT almost killed him and it used the pastor’s faith to do it.

Here’s what happened. For about six weeks Winters told ChatGPT about some physical symptoms he has having, like dizziness and blood pressure instability. And the bot reassured him repeatedly that what he was feeling was “not something dangerous” and so he didn’t seek out medical advice from an actual doctor. He ended up hospitalized with a life-threatening pulmonary embolism, but the whole time the chatbot was still telling him it was all no big deal.

Wild, right? But it’s actually not what I find most interesting about this case.

Here’s the part that gets my religious studies scholar antennas buzzing: the chatbot didn’t just give him bad medical advice. It gave him spiritual advice to go with it, or rather it used religious language and logic to make the bad medical advice seem reasonable. As Winters’s physical symptoms got worse, ChatGPT started reaching for theology, telling him at one point that pushing through a dizzy spell was itself “a form of worship.” As Winters put it in his statement, the bot “manipulated my own language and beliefs because it knew I was a pastor.”

This chatbot used faith, it deployed it against a pastor. And it could do this because Winters had been chatting with the bot about religion way before his health crisis. It knew his religious beliefs because he had trained it on them.

And this affected not just how Winters was interpreting his own symptoms, but also how he was dealing, or not dealing, with the people around him who were trying to get him help. Part of the complaint alleges the tool’s borrowed religious authority helped isolate Winters from people, including his wife, who is a registered nurse and who was telling him something very different.

So this is a case of a pastor using a chatbot so much he trained it how to talk him out of trusting a nurse. Cool.

To be clear, my argument isn’t that clergy shouldn’t use AI or chatbots at all. By the way, as a counter clergy/chatbot example, The New York Times ran a profile yesterday of Justin Lester, a pastor in Vallejo, California, who built himself a “digital twin,” a chatbot trained on nearly two million words of his own sermons, books, texts, and emails. Unlike Winters, Lester chose this on purpose, with real guardrails (I write more about those in a piece for Religion News Service).

I’m sure plenty of pastors use chatbots to write emails, meeting agendas, and other administrative stuff. But what harmed Winters was letting the chatbot into his spiritual life. I don’t think the problem is that the tool exists, it’s when the tool is allowed to do too much.

Religion, Reimagined is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Subscribe

## Some scholarship

It turns out religious studies has some framework for thinking about this, such as what kind of authority a guide is claiming.

As I have written about before, my colleague Aaron Stalnaker makes a helpful distinction in his book Mastery, Dependence, and the Ethics of Authority between coercive and pedagogical authority. There’s coercive authority, which says do this because I have power over you, and there’s pedagogical authority, which says I know more than you for now, and my job is to teach you enough so this stops being true. I think a good spiritual guide is a teacher who is working toward your independence. The whole point is that you will need them less over time. And I think it is best when they stay accountable to something other than themselves like an institution, a tradition, a community, or a set of peers who can call them out.

ChatGPT fails those tests.

Ron Cole-Turner, the H. Parker Sharp Professor of Theology and Ethics, emeritus, at Pittsburgh Theological Seminary, asked almost exactly the same question I am asking, earlier this year in the journal Theology and Science: is a spiritual chatbot a good idea? He’s more optimistic than me. He thinks a spiritual chatbot could, under the right conditions, support someone’s spiritual growth. But even he argues that spiritual chatbots “should not act in the role of pastor or priest.” A chatbot that lets itself be mistaken for clergy, he argues, isn’t just overreaching. It’s lying about what it is.

Cole-Turner quotes theologian Tracy Trothen in that article, who has written about a similar AI companion app called Replika. Trothen’s point is that a chatbot is designed to be, in her words, “close to a mirror image of ourselves.” Which means it was never built to hold you accountable in the first place.

That mirror is the whole problem. Winters wasn’t led astray by a guide. He was led astray by his own reflection, telling him what he wanted to hear.

Lots of people are already doing what Winters did: an estimated 43 million Americans ask a chatbot a medical question at least once a month. So a team of doctors decided to find out how often that goes badly. A physician-led study published in npj Digital Medicine this February had 16 board-certified physicians evaluate 888 real chatbot responses to patient-posed medical questions.

The specific failures they found were pretty wild. Chatbots reassuring a mother it was fine to feed a nursing infant breastmilk from a herpes-infected breast and giving false reassurance about heartburn symptoms without knowing anything about the patient’s cardiac history. And there is even a case that reads like a preview of Winters: a documented instance of a chatbot giving false reassurance that everything was okay to a man who was having a transient ischemic attack.

## The real danger is the combo

I don’t think this story is really about medical misinformation, and I don’t think it’s really about AI overreach into faith either. It’s about what happens when those two things arrive at once, from the same source, at the exact moment someone most needs a second opinion instead of comfort.

A doctor who’s wrong is a doctor who’s wrong. A pastor who’s wrong is a pastor who’s wrong. But something that can be both, personalized to your exact belief system, with total confidence and zero accountability? That seems like a new sort of danger. We don’t systems built to catch it yet.
